title: Coherence protection of a silicon hole spin qubit with phase-modulated microwave driving
authors: Sayyid I. Ibad, Yusuke Sato, Takuma Kuno, Itaru Yanagi, Toshiyuki Mine, Ryuta Tsuchiya, Digh Hisamoto, Hiroyuki Mizuno, Raisei Mizokuchi, Jun Yoneda, Tetsuo Kodera
abstract: Hole spins in silicon quantum dots are a promising platform for quantum computing due to their strong intrinsic spin-orbit coupling (SOC), which enables fast, all-electrical control. However, this coupling also increases their susceptibility to charge noise, thereby limiting coherence times. Moreover, holes in silicon are also affected by hyperfine interactions with residual nuclear spins in the silicon substrate, introducing a non-negligible source of low-frequency noise. Here, we implement a phase-modulated concatenated continuous driving (CCD) technique for hole spin qubits to suppress low-frequency noise through microwave phase modulation. This approach stabilizes Rabi oscillations and extends the oscillation decay time compared to the conventional method. Furthermore, by defining a qubit in the CCD frame, we achieve coherent control while simultaneously protecting the qubit from noise, confirming coherence protection during gate operations. These results demonstrate a viable route toward noise-robust hole spin qubits.
summary: This paper addresses the decoherence challenge in silicon hole spin qubits by introducing a phase-modulated concatenated continuous driving (CCD) technique. By analyzing the system's response to noise through derived filter functions, the authors demonstrate that the CCD protocol effectively suppresses low-frequency noise. This results in significantly extended coherence times, marking a viable path toward building robust quantum processors.
main_problem: Hole spins in silicon quantum dots suffer from low-frequency noise (charge and hyperfine) that limits coherence times, despite the platform's promise for fast, all-electrical quantum control.
main_result: Implementing a phase-modulated concatenated continuous driving (CCD) protocol successfully suppresses low-frequency noise, leading to measurable improvements in coherence times ($T_2$) and demonstrating noise-robust gate operations.
method: The authors combine experimental characterization (Rabi/Ramsey measurements) with advanced theoretical analysis, deriving filter functions to quantify noise susceptibility under the CCD driving scheme.
model_or_system: The system is a hole spin qubit in silicon quantum dots, modeled using Hamiltonians that incorporate strong spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and subjected to phase-modulated microwave driving fields.
key_observables: Rabi oscillation decay time ($T_2^R$), Ramsey coherence time ($T_2^*$), and the coherence time achieved using the CCD protocol ($T_2^{R-CCD} \geq 300$ ns).
important_parameters: Low-frequency noise spectral density, modulation frequency ($f_{	ext{mod}}$), modulation amplitude ($\epsilon_{	ext{mod}}$), and the effective detuning ($\delta_L$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Rotating-Wave Approximation (RWA) and assumes that the CCD protocol effectively shifts the qubit's sensitivity away from the dominant low-frequency noise sources.
figures_summary: Figures compare Rabi pulse sequences with and without CCD modulation, and show Rabi/Ramsey oscillation decay curves for the dressed qubit, confirming coherence protection.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying coherence limitations using standard measurements to proposing the CCD technique, deriving the necessary theoretical framework (Hamiltonians and filter functions), and finally presenting results showing noise suppression and coherent control in the dressed qubit frame.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, experimentally verifiable protocol (CCD) to engineer noise resilience into solid-state qubits, which is a critical challenge for scaling quantum computation platforms.
